set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 54-year-old has an intraocular pressure of 26 mmHg, but the optic nerve and visual fields are normal. What is this called?
opts: Normal pressure
26 is above the normal range.
Ocular hypertension
Correct — pressure above normal WITHOUT optic nerve damage or field loss. Normal runs about 10 to 21.
Open-angle glaucoma
Glaucoma implies optic nerve damage or field loss, which this patient does not have.
Angle-closure glaucoma
An abrupt blockage of the drainage canal, usually with acute pain.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A newborn needs prophylaxis against ophthalmia neonatorum. Which agent?
opts: Erythromycin ointment
Correct. It is the named agent for newborn prophylaxis, and it is inexpensive.
Azithromycin solution
Used for conjunctivitis, and considerably more expensive.
Moxifloxacin solution
A fluoroquinolone for conjunctivitis and ulcers.
Natamycin suspension
An antifungal.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 41-year-old man has used a vasoconstrictor drop for three days with no improvement in his red eye. What should he do?
opts: Continue for another week and reassess
Continuing past the point of failure risks rebound and delays a diagnosis.
Double the frequency
More frequent use worsens the rebound problem without addressing the cause.
Switch to a second vasoconstrictor
Changing brand does not change the class or the problem.
Stop the drop and see a provider
Correct. No improvement within 72 hours is the stated trigger for review. Because something more serious may be going on.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 30-year-old man has used an over-the-counter redness-relief drop every day for a month. His eyes are redder than when he started. What has happened?
opts: He has bacterial conjunctivitis
Nothing here suggests infection, and the timing follows the drop rather than an exposure.
The drops have raised his intraocular pressure
Raised pressure is a steroid and non-steroidal concern, not a vasoconstrictor one.
Rebound hyperaemia
Correct. Beyond about two weeks, stopping leaves the eye redder than it started. This is the counselling point most worth carrying out of this topic.
He has developed allergic conjunctivitis
Possible in general, but the history of daily vasoconstrictor use for a month points squarely at rebound.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 34-year-old has a dendritic corneal lesion consistent with herpes simplex keratitis. Which TOPICAL agent is available?
opts: Natamycin
An antifungal.
Trifluridine
Correct, and its ocular toxicity is punctate keratopathy. Ganciclovir is the other ophthalmic preparation.
Valacyclovir
An oral agent for simplex keratitis and zoster ophthalmicus, not a topical one.
Foscarnet
Intravenous, for cytomegalovirus retinitis.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 58-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis has chronic dry eye with inflammation. Beyond tear substitutes, which agent is indicated?
opts: Cyclosporine drops
Correct. It inhibits interleukin 2 production, reduces lacrimal inflammatory markers and raises tear production. Ocular burning is the commonest complaint.
A topical antihistamine
It would worsen matters — antihistamines INCREASE ocular dryness.
A vasoconstrictor
It treats redness short-term and risks rebound.
An ophthalmic antibiotic
There is no infection here.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 55-year-old has been using tobramycin drops for five days and now has worsening pain and a corneal defect. What has happened?
opts: Rebound hyperaemia
That follows vasoconstrictor use, not an antibiotic.
Corneal ulceration
Correct, along with reactive keratoconjunctivitis. It is one of the few ocular adverse effects specific enough to name a class.
Ordinary ocular irritation, common to all ophthalmic antibiotics
Irritation is indeed common to all of them, which is why it is NOT the answer when a specific defect has appeared.
A white precipitate from the drug
That belongs to ciprofloxacin and is a surface deposit, not an ulcer.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 68-year-old on a prostaglandin analogue still has inadequate pressure control. What is the principle for adding a second agent?
opts: Add a second prostaglandin analogue
Same mechanism gives no synergy.
Increase the prostaglandin to twice daily
That actively reduces its effect.
Add a topical steroid
Steroids raise intraocular pressure.
Add an agent with a DIFFERENT mechanism
Correct. Targeting a second route gives synergy, and fewer drops improves compliance. Which brand pairs which two drugs matters far less than the principle.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A parent struggles to get drops into a wriggling toddler's eye. What do you suggest, and what do you warn about?
opts: A drop given twice as often
More frequent dosing does not solve the administration problem.
An oral antibiotic instead
Systemic therapy is reserved for more involved infection.
A vasoconstrictor to reduce redness first
It treats appearance, not the underlying problem.
An ointment, which blurs vision briefly
Correct. Ointments suit children and poor compliance, and the blurring means no driving until it clears.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 60-year-old with a strong family history of glaucoma needs a topical steroid for anterior uveitis. What is the particular concern, and what might you choose?
opts: Raised intraocular pressure
Correct. Pressure elevation is more likely with a family history, and the soft steroids carry lower pressure risk. Consider a soft steroid such as loteprednol.
Cataract formation — choose difluprednate
Cataract is a real steroid risk, but the family history points specifically at pressure, and difluprednate is not a soft steroid.
Corneal ulceration — choose prednisolone
Ulcers are on the steroid risk list, but prednisolone is not the lower-risk option.
Rebound hyperaemia — avoid steroids entirely
Rebound hyperaemia belongs to the vasoconstrictors.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 22-year-old has watery, red eyes after a family member had the same. Adenoviral conjunctivitis is diagnosed. What is the treatment?
opts: Symptomatic relief of irritation
Correct. It runs a self-limited course. There is no antiviral for it.
Trifluridine drops
For herpes simplex keratitis and keratoconjunctivitis, not adenovirus.
Oral valacyclovir
For simplex keratitis and zoster ophthalmicus.
A topical fluoroquinolone
An antibacterial, which does nothing for a virus.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 38-year-old reports a foreign body sensation after gardening. Which agent reveals an epithelial defect?
opts: Tropicamide
A cycloplegic for dilation.
Phenylephrine
A mydriatic.
Fluorescein
Correct — it discloses corneal injury and stains the anterior segment.
Proparacaine
An anaesthetic, often used alongside it, but it does not stain.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 21-year-old contact lens wearer is treated for conjunctivitis. When may she resume her lenses?
opts: When the eye is not inflamed and there has been no discharge for 24 hours
Correct, and she should get rid of her eye makeup too. With the lens discarded or disinfected.
Immediately, as long as she is using drops
Lenses must be discontinued while the eye is inflamed.
After finishing the full antibiotic course, regardless of the eye
The criterion is the state of the eye, not the end of the course.
After 7 days in all cases
The rule is based on inflammation and discharge, not a fixed count.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 59-year-old starting cyclosporine drops should be warned about which common effect?
opts: Ocular burning
Correct, alongside foreign body sensation and blurred vision. In about one in six patients.
A bitter taste
That belongs to the carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Darkening of the iris
That belongs to the prostaglandin analogues.
Bradycardia
That is systemic beta blockade from a glaucoma drop.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 47-year-old farm worker develops fungal keratitis after a corneal injury with plant material. Which commercially available ophthalmic agent treats it?
opts: Trifluridine
An antiviral.
Natamycin
Correct — the only commercially available ophthalmic antifungal. It covers Aspergillus, Candida, Cephalosporium, Fusarium and Penicillium.
Amphotericin B drops
Used ophthalmically but not as a commercially available product; it must be compounded.
Oral fluconazole alone
Systemic azoles have a role, but the question asks for the available ophthalmic agent.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 29-year-old presents with an eye complaint. What must be done BEFORE instilling any medication?
opts: Stain with fluorescein
A diagnostic step that follows, not the universal first action.
Document a visual acuity
Correct, along with documenting allergies and the date and result of the last eye examination. Acuity is repeated at every follow-up.
Measure intraocular pressure
Useful in the right context, but acuity is the stated first step before any drug goes in.
Dilate the pupil
Dilation itself is a medication, and acuity comes first.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 28-year-old has itchy, watery eyes each spring and wants something that works today. Which class do you choose?
opts: An ophthalmic glucocorticoid
Reserved for refractory symptoms, and limited to a pulse of under two weeks.
An ophthalmic non-steroidal
Indicated for postoperative inflammation and allergic conjunctivitis, but not the first reach for acute itch.
An ophthalmic antihistamine
Correct, and they are typically preferred over mast cell stabilisers. Allow two weeks to judge full efficacy. Which works within minutes.
A mast cell stabiliser
It needs 5 to 14 days for full efficacy and is NOT useful for acute symptoms.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 62-year-old is newly diagnosed with open-angle glaucoma and has risk factors. Which class do you start?
opts: A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Effective, but not the stated first choice.
A topical glucocorticoid
Steroids RAISE intraocular pressure.
A prostaglandin analogue
Correct — first line and the most commonly used, dosed once daily. A beta blocker is the other reasonable start.
A cholinergic agonist
Poor compliance from side effects and frequent dosing.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: A 74-year-old on timolol drops for glaucoma develops systemic side effects. By what route did the drug reach the circulation?
opts: Transcorneal absorption into the bloodstream
Transcorneal absorption is what produces the LOCAL ocular effect.
Absorption through the eyelid skin
Eyelid skin is not the described route. It is the nasolacrimal duct.
Swallowed residue from the eyelashes
Swallowed residue is not the described mechanism; drainage down the nasolacrimal duct is.
Nasolacrimal drainage
Correct. What runs down the duct is absorbed systemically without passing through the liver first. Which also avoids first-pass metabolism.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: You are teaching a 72-year-old to use eye drops. What is the MOST important step?
opts: Holding a finger over the lacrimal duct
Important for drops, though unnecessary for gels and ointments.
Tilting the head back
Part of the technique, but not the step singled out.
Washing the hands
Correct, and it is singled out as the most important step of all.
Holding the eyes closed for 2 to 3 minutes
Important, and it limits systemic absorption, but not the step singled out as most important.

set1.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set1.q: At follow-up, a 61-year-old's documented visual acuity is worse than at the first visit. What does that require?
opts: Repeating the course of drops
Worsening acuity needs assessment, not more of the same treatment.
Reassurance and review in a week
Delay is precisely what the rule exists to prevent.
Switching to an ointment
Formulation is not the issue.
Immediate ophthalmology consult
Correct — which is the reason acuity is documented at every visit.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 27-year-old starting an ophthalmic antihistamine asks when she will know if it is working. What do you tell her?
opts: Allow 5 to 14 days before it works at all
That is the mast cell stabiliser timeline.
It should work fully within an hour
Onset is fast but full efficacy takes about two weeks.
Allow six weeks
Longer than the stated period.
It acts within minutes
Correct — fast onset, slower to reach full efficacy. But allow two weeks to judge the full effect.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 24-year-old woman asks how long she can keep using her redness-relief drops. What do you tell her?
opts: As long as her eyes stay red
That is exactly what produces rebound hyperaemia.
No more than six weeks
Well beyond the stated limit.
No more than two weeks
Correct, and if there is no improvement within 72 hours she should stop and be seen.
No more than 72 hours
72 hours is the point at which FAILURE should prompt review, not the limit on use.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 45-year-old needs pupil dilation for fundoscopy, and you want the pupil to stay as reactive to light as possible. Which agent?
opts: Atropine
An antimuscarinic with the longest action of the three.
Phenylephrine
Correct. The sympathomimetic leaves the pupil more reactive to light than an antimuscarinic does.
Tropicamide
An antimuscarinic; the pupil is less reactive.
Cyclopentolate
An antimuscarinic; the pupil is less reactive.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 6-year-old is prescribed ciprofloxacin drops. Two days later the parent reports a white deposit on the eye. What is this?
opts: A corneal ulcer forming
Ulceration is the aminoglycoside risk, and it would be painful rather than a surface deposit.
A fungal superinfection
Nothing here suggests fungus, and the timing follows the drug too closely.
Dried ointment residue
Ciprofloxacin here is a solution, and the precipitate is a known drug effect.
An expected white precipitate
Correct, and specific enough to ciprofloxacin to be worth warning about in advance. Seen in about one in six patients on this drug.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 33-year-old asks for a prescription for the numbing drops that helped during foreign body removal. What do you do?
opts: Decline — not for home use
Correct. The eye stays numb for 10 to 20 minutes with no blink reflex, which is unsafe unsupervised.
Prescribe a short course for comfort
Explicitly not to be prescribed.
Prescribe them with a warning not to drive
The problem is the absent blink reflex, not driving alone, and they are not dispensed.
Substitute a topical steroid
A different drug for a different purpose, with its own risks.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 19-year-old contact lens wearer has purulent conjunctivitis. Keratitis has been excluded. Which class do you reach for, and why?
opts: A fluoroquinolone
Correct, and the same class is preferred for corneal ulcers for the same reason. Because lens wearers are at high risk for Pseudomonas.
A macrolide, because it is soothing on the inflamed eye
Erythromycin is soothing and cheap, but it does not cover the organism this patient is at risk from.
An aminoglycoside, because it covers gram negatives
Its risk of corneal ulceration makes it a poor choice in an eye already at risk.
Sulfacetamide, because it is inexpensive
Cost is not the deciding factor when Pseudomonas is the concern.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman starting a prostaglandin analogue in one eye should be warned about which cosmetic effects?
opts: Drooping of the eyelid
Not an effect attributed to prostaglandin analogues here.
Longer lashes and iris colour change
Correct, and they matter more when only one eye is treated. Conjunctival hyperaemia is common too.
Yellowing of the sclera
Yellowing of the sclera is not an effect of the prostaglandin analogues.
Permanent pupil dilation
Permanent dilation is not an effect of this class; the changes are to lashes and iris colour.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 51-year-old is prescribed a topical steroid for anterior uveitis. How long may the course run?
opts: Less than 72 hours
Shorter than the stated limit.
Less than two weeks, as a pulse
Correct. The risks — cataract, raised pressure, infection, delayed healing, corneal ulcers — are why.
Up to three months
Far beyond the stated limit.
As long as inflammation persists
That is exactly what the pulse limit exists to prevent.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 57-year-old needs treatment for endophthalmitis with an immediate local effect. Which route achieves this by circumventing absorption entirely?
opts: Subconjunctival injection
Prompt or sustained, but it does not circumvent absorption.
Oral therapy
The slowest route to the eye of those listed.
Intravitreal injection or device
Correct, with a potential sustained effect too. Its limitation is retinal toxicity.
Topical drops
Prompt but formulation-dependent, and much is lost to drainage.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 26-year-old finds his vision blurs badly on pilocarpine. Why is this class particularly poorly tolerated in younger patients?
opts: It causes iris colour change in the young
That belongs to the prostaglandin analogues.
Miosis blurs vision
Correct — fixed small pupils, myopia and visual disturbance, and compliance suffers for it.
Younger patients absorb more drug systemically
Systemic absorption is not greater in the young. The stated reason is the visual blurring itself.
The drug raises intraocular pressure in the young
It lowers pressure by increasing outflow.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: An 18-month-old needs pressure-lowering therapy. Which class is contraindicated?
opts: Prostaglandin analogues
Prostaglandin analogues carry no stated age contraindication; the under-two rule is the alpha-2 agonists.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
Their problems are taste and stinging.
Cholinergic agonists
Their problems are miosis and blurring.
Alpha-2 agonists
Correct — contraindicated under two years because of central nervous system depression and apnoea.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 40-year-old is shown how to use both a drop and an ointment. Why must she cover the lacrimal duct after the DROP but not the ointment?
opts: The ointment is absorbed entirely through the cornea
Corneal absorption is not the reason. It is the viscosity: the ointment does not drain away.
Ointments have no systemic absorption at all
The reason given is that it does not go anywhere, rather than a claim of zero absorption.
Drops are sterile and ointments are not
Both are handled aseptically.
The ointment is too viscous to drain away
Correct. With a drop, occluding the duct limits nasolacrimal drainage and the systemic absorption that follows it. So there is nothing to block.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A toddler swallows a bottle of a parent's redness-relief drops. Why is this dangerous, given the drug acts on alpha-1 receptors in the eye?
opts: Systemically they act on alpha-2
Correct. Local alpha-1 against systemic alpha-2 is exactly why an ingestion behaves differently from an instillation.
Systemically they act on beta-1 receptors
Beta-1 is the cardiac target of the beta blocker drops, not these.
They are converted to epinephrine in the gut
Dipivefrin is the prodrug converted to epinephrine, and that happens in the eye.
They inhibit carbonic anhydrase systemically
That is the mechanism of a different glaucoma class.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 66-year-old on latanoprost asks whether using it twice daily would lower his pressure further. What do you tell him?
opts: Yes, but only if pressure remains high
Frequency above once daily reduces the effect regardless of pressure.
It makes no difference either way
It actively reduces the benefit.
No — it INHIBITS the effect
Correct, and counterintuitive enough to be worth stating plainly.
Yes, twice daily is more effective
The opposite is true here: exceeding once daily reduces the pressure-lowering effect.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 71-year-old on dorzolamide complains of a persistent bitter taste and stinging on instillation. What do you tell him?
opts: Both are common with this class
Correct, and they are common enough that warning in advance improves adherence. Bitter taste in about a quarter and stinging in about a third.
This suggests an allergy and the drug must stop
Allergic conjunctivitis can occur, but taste and stinging are expected effects.
This means the drop is contaminated
No — they are known effects of the drug.
This indicates systemic absorption and cardiac risk
Cardiac risk belongs to the beta blockers.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 70-year-old on timolol drops develops fatigue and a heart rate of 48. What has happened?
opts: An allergic reaction to the preservative
It would not produce bradycardia.
Rebound hyperaemia
A vasoconstrictor effect, and it does not affect heart rate.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition
A different class, with taste and stinging as its problems.
Systemic beta blockade
Correct. Worsening heart failure, bradycardia, heart block and increased airway resistance are all possible from a drop.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 58-year-old with asthma needs a beta blocker drop for glaucoma. Which agent, and why?
opts: Levobunolol, because it is well tolerated
Also nonselective.
Carteolol, because it is beta-2 selective
It is nonselective, and a beta-2 selective blocker is not what you would want anyway.
Betaxolol — beta-1 selective
Correct. The nonselective agents are more efficacious in the eye but carry the respiratory risk.
Timolol, because it is more efficacious
Nonselective, and its increased airway resistance is exactly the problem here.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 35-year-old with predictable seasonal allergy cannot tolerate antihistamine drops and is willing to start weeks before the season. Which class suits her?
opts: An ophthalmic antibiotic
There is no infection to treat.
A mast cell stabiliser
Correct. Slow to work — 5 to 14 days — but that matters less when treatment starts before the season.
A vasoconstrictor used daily through the season
Prolonged use causes rebound hyperaemia.
A topical glucocorticoid through the season
Steroids are limited to pulses of under two weeks.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 63-year-old is being assessed for a corneal infiltrate. Which of her features most raises the risk that it is FUNGAL?
opts: Long-term topical steroid use
Correct. Immunosuppression — including topical steroids — sits alongside trauma, chronic surface disease and contact lens wear.
A history of migraine
No stated relationship to ocular fungal infection.
Taking a beta blocker for hypertension
Antihypertensive therapy is not among the listed risk factors for ocular fungal infection.
Wearing reading glasses
Spectacles are not a risk factor. Contact lens WEAR is, alongside trauma and immunosuppression.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 36-year-old has a small peripheral corneal infection. Why can a topical antibiotic reach concentrations at the eye that an intravenous one cannot?
opts: The cornea actively transports antibiotics
Transcorneal absorption is passive and governed by the concentration gradient.
Topical drugs avoid the blood-brain barrier
The blood-brain barrier is not what separates topical from systemic delivery to the eye.
It gives very high LOCAL concentrations
Correct — and the trade-off is that more involved infection still needs systemic therapy.
Topical drugs have greater systemic bioavailability
The opposite: systemic bioavailability from a drop is limited.

set2.io: Ophthalmic drugs — indications, adverse effects, contraindications and patient education
set2.q: A 44-year-old with a documented sulfonamide allergy needs treatment for bacterial conjunctivitis. Which agent must be avoided?
opts: Sulfacetamide
Correct. It is a sulfonamide, so the allergy rules it out.
Bacitracin
A cell wall agent with no sulfonamide component.
Erythromycin
A macrolide, unrelated to sulfonamides.
Tobramycin
An aminoglycoside, unrelated to sulfonamides.
